transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO, NimbleSearch), Elena Torres (ML Eng), Carlos Diaz (Infra)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC throughput runs, continuous batching experiments and concurrency targets. Reviewed recent benchmark numbers (link shared), discussed queueing behavior at high concurrency, and next steps to run longer continuous-batching windows and validate 95th pct latency SLO.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this to about 45-ish minutes and then any questions, um Maya and I are here to walk through the latest runs.
[00:08] Rajiv: thanks samir, appreciate it. quick ask up front — we want to make sure the numbers you're showing are representative of our prod pattern which has a fairly spiky QPS.
[00:15] Maya: totally, we brought the 10m window that matches the bursts you sent earlier. we ran continuous batching for 30 minutes last thursday, and there's a couple of artifacts to call out — the KV cache warmup, and a small tail latency bump when queueing starts at about 3k concurrent requests.
[00:30] Elena: that matches what we saw in our probe, we saw 95th jump from 220ms to ~360ms at the same time.
[00:36] Samir: ok so let's put numbers on the table, the run we shared in the spreadsheet (link pasted in chat) — average throughput 4.2k tokens/sec across the pool, median latency ~120ms, p95 ~260ms overall, but during the burst segment where queue length hit ~800 requests, p95 spiked to 360ms.
[01:02] Carlos: can you remind me what the pool config was for that run? model variant, batch sizing, and number of GPUs?
[01:07] Maya: yes, that run was hosted pilot: r-infer-3b quantized int8, 4xA10 equivalent, concurrent clients simulated at up to 4k, batching window 20ms (continuous mode), max batch cap set to 512 tokens, and KV cache enabled with a 90% hit assumption.
[01:24] Rajiv: hmm r-infer-3b int8 — any expected quality regressions? our evaluation set showed a small drop on one grammar-sensitive task but acceptable overall.
[01:33] Maya: we noted a 1.8% drop on that specific eval, but most endpoints were within the target quality threshold you defined. we can try fp16 for a follow-up to check perf delta.
[01:42] Samir: more importantly for this thread — the throughput vs latency tradeoff. continuous batching gave us better token/sec, but when concurrency crosses the pooling threshold we see queueing and tail latency. there are a couple of levers: increase concurrency headroom (more GPUs/dedicated), tune batch flush thresholds, or use aggressive pre-batching for predictable patterns.
[02:01] Elena: can you explain pre-batching? we thought continuous batching was already doing that.
[02:06] Maya: good q — continuous batching keeps a small micro-window (e.g., 10-25ms) to accumulate requests before a kernel launch. pre-batching here refers to routing policy where upstream client aggregators send already coalesced requests when they detect a burst, so the runtime sees fewer, larger batches and reduces queueing overhead.
[02:24] Rajiv: ok, so that requires infra changes on our side?
[02:27] Maya: minimal if you already have a gateway — it can be a small shim that buffers for X ms or until N requests. we can share a reference implementation.
[02:34] Samir: action item for us to share that shim — we have a snippet in the repo. link: https://git.redwood.dev/poc/nimble/prebatch-shim
[02:40] Carlos: nice. from infra perspective our prefered path is avoiding horizontal scale up if possible since cost is sensitive. what about queueing configs? can you do request shedding or dynamic thresholds?
[02:50] Maya: yes, runtime supports soft queue limits and backpressure: we can return a 429 at the ingress, or we can prioritize requests (e.g., route HQ traffic to dedicated lanes). there's also an adaptive batching mode that reduces window size when queue depth grows to bound latency.
[03:07] Rajiv: what about KV cache warmup? you mentioned a 90% assumed hit rate — in our prod it's more like 60% initially.
[03:15] Maya: that will impact effective throughput; lower hit rate means more forward passes and larger effective compute. we can model that — in our spreadsheet we included columns for cache hit 60/80/90. i'll highlight the 60% line in the updated dashboard.
[03:28] Elena: can we also see per-request token distributions? some of our calls are 2-token prompts + 512 tokens output, others are shorter; average token-per-request matters a lot for batching efficiency.
[03:38] Maya: yep included in sample traces, but send a larger slice of production traces (anonymized) and we'll run a more representative sim.
[03:45] Samir: quick note on concurrency target — your stated target was 10k concurrent users for peak, correct?
[03:50] Rajiv: roughly, but concurrency here means active in-flight requests — our 10k converts to about 3.5k concurrent requests at peak given user think time, but we wanted headroom to 5k in the pilot.
[04:02] Maya: ok so current runs at simulated 4k concurrency exercised that range. main recommendation: aim for two modes — baseline hosted with continuous batching tuned for cost, and dedicated pilot with more headroom for spikes if p95 requirement is strict.
[04:17] Carlos: what's the expected unit cost difference if we move to Dedicated 8xA10 vs hosted bursts?
[04:22] Samir: ballpark: hosted per-token cost is higher at low to mid scale because of multi-tenant overhead, Dedicated fixed monthly + lower per-token. in the spreadsheet we show estimated unit cost at 50M tokens/month: hosted ~ $0.018/token-equivalent unit, Dedicated provisioned ~ $0.012, rough numbers, will attach formal pricing.
[04:40] Elena: ok useful. any immediate tuning we can do without changing infra?
[04:44] Maya: yes — lower batch flush window to 10-15ms for the bursty endpoints, enable adaptive batching, and tighten the KV cache TTL tuning so warmups persist across sessions for longer. those three are config flips on our side.
[04:58] Rajiv: if we lower window to 10ms won't throughput drop?
[05:02] Maya: median token/sec may drop slightly, but tail latency improves; the net cost per useful token could improve if more requests meet latency SLO without needing more GPUs. it's an empirical tradeoff so we'd test.
[05:15] Samir: question from my side — did the team observe any outlier errors during the 30-minute run? any OOMs or internal retries?
[05:21] Maya: a couple of transient kernel retries when batch size hit the top cap, but nothing actionable — we saw automatic retry and success. will include logs.
[05:30] Carlos: we also care about cold starts for the private pilot — how long to spin up a node and warm KV?
[05:36] Maya: cold start for a new shard around ~45-90s depending on model size; KV warm to steady-state maybe 5-10 minutes under representative traffic. for private on-prem we can keep warm replica pools to reduce startup.
[05:50] Rajiv: good. can we get a targeted experiment plan — what exactly will you run and when?
[05:55] Samir: yes, proposal: Maya will run 1-hour continuous-batching test at 4k concurrency with three variants: (A) window 20ms (baseline), (B) window 10ms + adaptive batching, (C) window 20ms + pre-batching shim. collect p50/p95/p99 token latencies, queue depth, batch size distribution, KV hit rates. we'll correlate with cost estimates.
[06:18] Elena: sounds good. please include raw logs and a small set of example traces we can replay.
[06:22] Maya: will do.
[06:24] Rajiv: any concerns around SSO/audit or the dedicated pilot that we should prep for?
[06:28] Samir: separate thread for security — we already shared SOC2 docs, but for Dedicated/Private we'll need SAML metadata and network peering details; Carlos mentioned a peering window next tuesday.
[06:39] Carlos: yep ops has a short window, we'll confirm.
[06:42] Maya: also quick callout — if you want to minimize cost while meeting latency target, quantization profiles matter; int8 was cheap but had small quality drop; fp16 will likely increase throughput slightly at cost delta. we'll run an fp16 comparison in the next run if you want.
[06:57] Rajiv: yes add fp16 run as option D.
[07:00] Samir: perfect. i'll update the run matrix in the sheet and share.
[07:04] Elena: timeline — when can we expect results?
[07:07] Samir: maya can run today/tomorrow; results and dashboard by Friday 2026-03-06. then we regroup early next week to review and discuss Dedicated sizing.
[07:18] Maya: one more micro point — if queueing persists at target concurrency we can enable prioritized lanes for key endpoints, that reduces p95 for critical flows while offloading lower-priority to cheaper pools.
[07:29] Rajiv: that might be the right tradeoff for search relevance endpoint.
[07:33] Samir: ok final recap: Maya runs experiments A/B/C (+optional D fp16), Samir sends pricing and updated dashboard, customer provides sample traces and confirms peering window. meet next Tuesday Mar 10 for dedicated sizing deep dive.
[07:50] Rajiv: thanks all, appreciate the clear plan.
[07:53] Samir: thanks team — we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[07:56] (call ends)
